why: A link checker fails open in silence: a form it does not read, a finding it drops, or a run over no files all look exactly like a tree whose links resolve. Each edit below removes one of the protections the checker claims — a link form, the anchor rule, the quoting rules that keep examples out of the report, the empty-run refusal, and the path the verdict takes to the exit code.

mutations.name: the inline-link pattern stops matching
mutations.breaks: The oldest rule here, disabled by a regex that no longer fires. Every inline link reads clean because none is seen.

mutations.name: a missing target is not a problem
mutations.breaks: The file is resolved, found not to exist, and the finding is thrown away — the check runs and reports nothing.

mutations.name: the anchor check is dropped
mutations.breaks: A link to a real file with a fragment that names no heading lands at the top of the page instead, and nothing says so.

mutations.name: HTML image sources are not read
mutations.breaks: The form the README writes its two hero pictures in. This is exactly the gap the checker shipped with: an image whose file was renamed showed a broken picture on the front page and passed.

mutations.name: a multi-line tag is read only as far as its first line
mutations.breaks: The README writes one attribute per line, so a src on the second line is invisible to a line-bound reader and the tag is silently skipped.

mutations.name: HTML hrefs are not read
mutations.breaks: A badge or a picture wrapped in <a href> can point anywhere, including at a file that was deleted.

mutations.name: reference definitions are collected and never checked
mutations.breaks: A `[label]: target` line is where a reference link's target actually lives, and where a renamed file breaks every use of the label at once.

mutations.name: a reference with no definition is accepted
mutations.breaks: An unmatched label renders as literal brackets: the words stay on the page and the link is simply gone, which is the hardest kind of broken link to see by reading.

mutations.name: fenced code is scanned as prose
mutations.breaks: The other direction: a checker that reports every example link in every code block produces noise people learn to scroll past.

mutations.name: code spans are scanned as prose
mutations.breaks: Same noise from the other quoting form — a `[a][b]` written about code becomes a broken reference.

mutations.name: a run that found no files reports clean
mutations.breaks: Nothing to check and checked-and-clean are different answers. A checker that can pass by having nothing to look at is not a gate.

mutations.name: the findings are computed and then reported as clean
mutations.breaks: Every rule above works and the verdict never reaches the exit code. This is why the self-test goes through main() rather than calling check() and reading its list.
mutations.find:
print(f"check-doc-links: {len(problems)} broken link(s) in {len(files)} file(s)", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
mutations.replace:
print(f"check-doc-links: {len(problems)} broken link(s) in {len(files)} file(s)", file=sys.stderr)
        return 0

mutations.name: each file's findings are dropped as it is scanned
mutations.breaks: The scan visits every file and keeps none of what it found, so the report is a clean tree built from a complete pass.

mutations.name: the script's entry point is neutered
mutations.breaks: The verdict never reaches an exit code. A self-test that imported the module would stay green while the script itself always passed.
